seo.title: Luxbox — Product design case study | Max Zlydar
seo.description: Lead product design for a multichain trading terminal in the Blum ecosystem—from Telegram MVP to 2M+ activated traders and 300K DAU on a new platform UI.
seo.keywords: Luxbox, iGaming, rewards platform, product design, UX, UI, referral, case study, Max Zlydar
seo.ogTitle: Luxbox — Product design case study | Max Zlydar

intro.title: Blum trading hub is a young startup within Blum.io, specializing in developing Telegram bots for memecoin trading.

cover.challengeText: Create a multichain trading terminal to replace the old Telegram bot for the Blum ecosystem with 90M users.

problem.title: Problem
problem.body: The Telegram interface scared off potential customers. It was successful among a small circle of traders, but scaling such a product was difficult.

competitors.title: Nobody really knew the right way to do it.
competitors.body: The field is young, less than a year old. Competitors were navigating this path for the first time, without looking back, borrowing a lot from traditional trading.

intersection.body: Copying competitors' solutions was risky: Dynamic market, raw products, everything changed every month!

mvp.body: Based on the Telegram bot interface, the team assembled an MVP design in a month. No components, no styles, no auto-layouts. And no designer.

designSystem.body: The task for designers sounded like this: Apply the design system from the main service, draw edge cases and hand off to development.

insight.label: Interesting insight
insight.headline: In trading, the exchange makes money on commissions.
insight.detail: Up to 80% of profit comes from a dozen major traders who trade directly via API. Other players often make asset purchase decisions based on emotions. Two things matter here:
insight.item1: Emotions need to be triggered (indicators and casino-style)
insight.item2: Ability to buy instantly while emotions are still hot
insight.speedLine: Speed is helped by ⚡ Quickbuy. One-click buy and sell.

tokenCompetitor.body: And the "I'll get lucky now" feeling is activated by a frightening amount of pseudo-indicators on the token page. Also, competitors aren't afraid to go small: many components are 12px tall.

tokenOurs.body: In adapting our design system, we tried to find a compromise between analysis and emotions, between scale and informativeness. Important stuff first, the rest later.

final.title: Final result
final.body: Key indicators and a purchase widget fit on the main screen, allowing one-click buy and sell from the token screen.

buyModal.body: In one iteration, you could expand the widget and configure the transaction in more detail right in the modal window without loading new components, but due to technical limitations, we made the purchase in a separate window.

wallet.body: Wallet manager — a space for working with dozens of wallets across dozens of blockchains. There's no convenient way to work with hundreds of coins — but they can be converted and withdrawn as SOL/TON or stablecoins.

waitlist.body: Before launching the service, we created a waitlist and actively funneled all traffic here using the Telegram bot and social networks.

seo.title: Omni Optimise — Product design case study | Max Zlydar
seo.description: How a small task-status icon and clearer UX cut support engineers’ workload on Blum from roughly 70% down to about 15%—a focused product design case study.
seo.keywords: Omni Optimise, retail planogram, B2B, product design, UX, SaaS, case study, Max Zlydar
seo.ogTitle: Omni Optimise — Product design case study | Max Zlydar

intro.title:
How a small icon in task statuses reduced support engineer
workload from 70% → 15%.

cover.challengeText: Reduce support workload by making task completion statuses clearer.
cover.resultsText: Share of tickets related to task completion verification dropped from 75 → 15% among all support requests.

problem.title: Problem
problem.body: Completed tasks took a long time to validate and the spinner users saw after completion could spin for up to 24 hours. Users worried they wouldn't get their reward and went to complain to support.

intersection.body: But we couldn't touch the backend — any small change turned into a multi-week cohort rollout (90M users is no joke)

context.body: The task was small, but no one took it on due to massive workload across all tracks + all designers were on vacation. Had to move fast. To save time, I started by cutting the unnecessary.

solutions.title: Solution options
solutions.body: Created about 7 solutions from design system patterns. Selected the most adequate: Banner appearing over tasks; popover on hover over changed icon; top notification and modal.

testing.title: Testing
testing.body: Of all options, only one didn't interrupt the main flow, didn't distract users from other actions, and appeared only on request. We tested it with a focus group, where 77% immediately understood what the icon meant (survey).

colors.title: Color alternatives
colors.body: We explored alternative color schemes, but bright tones looked odd for hints + some resembled errors.

final.title: Rolled out two solutions at once:
final.body: Now: if task verification took more than 7 seconds, we changed the spinner to a clock icon on the frontend + gave a hint on click.

results.title: Result
results.summary: Share of tickets related to task completion verification was up to 75% among all support requests. We reduced it to 15%.
results.timeline: Task was done and rolled out to all users in 3 days.

seo.title: ShopBack — Product design case study | Max Zlydar
seo.description: Reworking levels and subscription UX for clearer progression and stronger conversion to paid plans—research-led product design case study by Max Zlydar.
seo.keywords: ShopBack, BNPL, fintech, payments, UX, product design, case study, Max Zlydar
seo.ogTitle: ShopBack — Product design case study | Max Zlydar

intro.title: Blum levels redesign that improved subscription conversion.

team.myRoleDesc: Product designer responsible for levels UX/UI

role.label: Challenge:
role.value: Users didn’t understand how levels worked, why they mattered, or how they affected the subscription — and conversion suffered.

cover.dataTitle: What we saw in the data
cover.dataText: A large share of users dropped off one or two steps before subscribing. Interviews showed people didn’t understand what levels gave them or how far they had progressed.
cover.hypothesisText: If we make the level system transparent and tie it to concrete value (bonuses, limits, perks), users can decide on a subscription more easily.

changes.title: What we changed
changes.desc1: Simpler progress logic, a clear visual level path, and plain descriptions of what unlocks at each stage.
changes.desc2: We emphasized actions that move users forward: completing tasks, trading, and engaging with the product.

next.title: What’s next
next.body: The full case covers hypotheses, level maps, A/B tests, and impact on key metrics. Reach out if you’d like a detailed walkthrough.
